# Burns and scalds

Kitchen and campfire first aid, from the school nurse's chart.

## Hot liquid scalds

Take the child or adult away from the heat and take off wet clothing and jewelry near the area, unless it is stuck to the skin. Cool the skin under cool running water for 20 minutes. Cover loosely with a clean, non-fluffy cloth or kitchen film. Leave any blisters alone; they protect the skin underneath. Do not put ice, butter, oil or toothpaste on a burn.

## Sunburn

Take a cool shower, apply aloe or an unscented moisturizer, and drink extra fluids. Sunburn that blisters is a second-degree burn: let the blisters heal, keep the skin covered, and stay out of the sun. See a doctor if there is fever, chills or a large area of blistering.

## Chemical burns

Brush off any dry powder, then flush the skin with cool running water for at least 20 minutes, taking contaminated clothing off as you go. Call poison control or 911 and bring the container.

## Electrical burns

Do not touch the person until the power is off. Call 911: the damage under the skin is usually worse than it looks.

## When a burn needs emergency care

Go to the emergency department for a burn larger than the palm of the person's hand, a burn on the face, hands, feet, groin or over a joint, any burn in a baby, or a burn that looks white, leathery or charred. Cool the burn while you wait.
